claims.text: The starting material is a multi-element, nearly equiatomic automotive alloy catalyst without additional dopants.
Introducing a minor amount of cerium during synthesis will form integrated, dispersed CeO2 nano-domains.
The resulting CeO2 nano-domains will be located at the catalyst surface and metal-oxide interfaces.
CeO2 exhibits reversible Ce3+/Ce4+ redox behavior associated with oxygen-vacancy formation.
CeO2 nano-domains will enhance oxygen storage, oxygen release, and redox buffering in the catalyst.
The CeO2 domains will undergo a quasi-zero-strain redox cycle.
Oxygen vacancies generated by the CeO2 domains will protect active sites from deactivation caused by H2O and NO.
CeO2-derived redox buffering and oxygen vacancies will protect active sites during thermal aging.
CeO2-associated oxygen mobility and vacancies can promote oxidation reaction kinetics.
Cerium incorporation will improve catalytic activity without increasing platinum-group-metal consumption.
The Ce-doped catalyst will have a lower light-off temperature than the untreated catalyst.
The Ce-doped catalyst will have a higher turnover frequency than the untreated catalyst.
The Ce-doped catalyst will retain activity better during long-term operation and thermal aging than the untreated catalyst.
The predicted improvements will hold below 500 °C under transient gasoline or hybrid-vehicle exhaust containing H2O and NO.
The predicted improvements may not apply at substantially higher temperatures or in drastically different chemical environments.
An optimal cerium concentration is needed to obtain integrated CeO2 domains without disrupting alloy uniformity.
Accelerated thermal aging can represent catalyst degradation associated with increasing vehicle mileage.
